claim: A fungus was found growing on the surface of the stem of the Aglaia odorata plant.
source: we identified a fungus growing on the surface of the stem of the Aglaia odorata plant with tremendous vitality (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the fungus on the plant.

claim: The Aglaia-infecting fungus belongs to the Ophiocordyceps genus.
source: This Aglaia-infecting fungus belonged to the Ophiocordyceps genus, which is known as zombie-ant fungus (Andersen et al., 2009; Araújo and Hughes, 2019; de Bekker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations to prior work on Ophiocordyceps.

claim: Ophiocordyceps genus is known as zombie-ant fungus.
source: This Aglaia-infecting fungus belonged to the Ophiocordyceps genus, which is known as zombie-ant fungus (Andersen et al., 2009; Araújo and Hughes, 2019; de Bekker et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Among the top 30 BLASTn hits using ITS as a query, 29 were from Ophiocordyceps species.
source: We performed a BLASTn search (Camacho et al., 2009) using the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) between rRNAs as a query and found that, among all the deposited nucleotide sequences in the database, 29 of the top 30 hits were from Ophiocordyceps species (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on BLASTn search results, which is a computational analysis of sequence data.

claim: The Aglaia-infecting fungus is distinct from other species of Ophiocordyceps.
source: This analysis indicated that the Aglaia-infecting fungus was distinct from the other species of Ophiocordyceps (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Aglaia-infecting fungus was positioned on a long branch separated from the most closely related strain, O. coccidiicola NBRC 100682, as supported by the 95% bootstrap value.
source: In particular, the strain isolated from Aglaia was positioned on a long branch separated from the most closely related strain, O. coccidiicola NBRC 100682, as supported by the 95% bootstrap value.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis with bootstrap support values.

claim: The fungus was named Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1.
source: we named the fungus Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 (Berkeley, Ryan Muller, strain 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 is closely related to known endophytic Ophiocordyceps spp.
source: Consistent with its isolation from the Aglaia plant, this fungus was closely related to known endophytic Ophiocordyceps spp. (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 3; Wang et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: Aglaia plants achieve self-resistance to rocaglates by introducing an amino acid substitution in eIF4A.
source: This self-resistance is achieved by the unique amino acid substitutions at the sites in eIF4A proteins where rocaglates directly associate (Iwasaki et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A possesses an amino acid conversion at the same residue as in the Aglaia plant eIF4A.
source: Remarkably, we observed an amino acid conversion in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A at the same residue as in the Aglaia plant eIF4A.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment data.

claim: A Gly residue replaced Phe163 (human position) in all four transcript isoforms in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1.
source: A Gly residue replaced Phe163 (human position) in all four transcript isoforms (from the same eIF4A gene) in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whereas His residues prevailed in the close kin of Ophiocordyceps species and other fungi.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in figures.

claim: His residues prevailed at position 163 (human position) in the close kin of Ophiocordyceps species and other fungi.
source: A Gly residue replaced Phe163 (human position) in all four transcript isoforms (from the same eIF4A gene) in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whereas His residues prevailed in the close kin of Ophiocordyceps species and other fungi.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in figures.

claim: RocA clamped human eIF4A1 on polypurine RNA ([AG]10) in an ATP-independent manner with Kd = ~0.42 µM.
source: rocaglamide A (RocA), a natural rocaglate derivative isolated from Aglaia plants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Janprasert et al., 1992), clamped human eIF4A1 on polypurine RNA ([AG]10) in an ATP-independent manner (e.g., in the presence of ADP + Pi) (Kd = ~0.42 µM, Figure 2C, left, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarization assay data shown in figures and tables.

claim: O. sinensis eIF4A showed high affinity for polypurine RNA with Kd = ~0.11 µM in the presence of RocA.
source: Whereas a high affinity for polypurine RNA was observed for eIF4A from O. sinensis (CO18 GCA 000448365) (Kd = ~0.11 µM, Figure 2C middle; Figure 2—figure supplement 2D; and Table 1)
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarization assay data shown in figures and tables.

claim: Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A showed a fairly high Kd (~17 µM) for polypurine RNA in the presence of RocA.
source: Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A showed a fairly high Kd (~17 µM, Figure 2C, right, Figure 2—figure supplement 2H, and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarization assay data shown in figures and tables.

claim: The Gly-to-Phe and Gly-to-His substitutions in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A sensitized the protein to RocA.
source: Indeed, both the Gly-to-Phe (human) and Gly-to-His (O. sinensis) substitutions in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A (Gly172Phe and Gly172His, respectively) sensitized the protein to RocA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and G), significantly reducing the Kd (Figure 2C, right, and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarization assay data shown in figures and tables.

claim: Introduction of a Gly residue into human and O. sinensis eIF4As reduced the affinity for polypurine RNA.
source: Conversely, introduction of a Gly residue into human and O. sinensis eIF4As reduced the affinity for polypurine RNA (Figure 2C, left, middle; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and E, and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarization assay data shown in figures and tables.

claim: The Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A evades rocaglate targeting by substituting a critical amino acid involved in its binding.
source: we concluded that the Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A evades rocaglate targeting by substituting a critical amino acid involved in its binding.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical data presented.

claim: When Phe163 was replaced by Gly in the crystal structure of the human eIF4A1•RocA complex, the π-π stacking with ring C of RocA was totally lost.
source: When Phe163 was replaced by Gly in the crystal structure of the human eIF4A1•RocA complex (Iwasaki et al., 2019), the π-π stacking with ring C of RocA was totally lost (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), likely leading to reduced affinity for RocA.
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling using a published crystal structure.

claim: The mechanism to desensitize eIF4A to rocaglates in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 is distinct from the Leu substitution found in Aglaia.
source: This mechanism to desensitize eIF4A to rocaglates was distinct from the Leu substitution found in Aglaia, which fills the space of the rocaglate binding pocket and thus prevents the interaction (Iwasaki et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with prior work on Aglaia eIF4A.

claim: eIF4A with His at position 163 (human position) is also a target of rocaglate.
source: Our data showed that eIF4A with His at position 163 (human position) is also a target of rocaglate (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarization assay data shown in figures and tables.

claim: The His substitution in human and Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4As was accompanied by an attenuated potency of RocA compared to the Phe substitution.
source: Although compared to the Phe substitution, the His substitution in human and Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4As was accompanied by an attenuated potency of RocA (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, and Table 1)
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarization assay data shown in figures and tables.

claim: A wide array of fungi that possess the His variant at position 163 are susceptible to rocaglates.
source: our data suggested that a wide array of fungi that possess the His variant (Figure 2A), including C. orbiculare (see below for details), are also susceptible to rocaglates.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the biochemical data and sequence alignments.

claim: Replacing wild-type human eIF4A1 with the Phe163Gly mutant prevented the translation repression mediated by RocA.
source: In contrast, replacing wild-type human eIF4A1 with the Phe163Gly mutant prevented the translation repression mediated by RocA (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is based on in vitro translation assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A could not alter translation in the preformed complex assay.
source: Whereas WT Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A could not alter translation (Figure 3B, left) due to its weaker ability to clamp on polypurine RNAs
evidence: The claim is based on in vitro translation assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Gly172His mutant of Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A could act as a translation repressor.
source: the Gly172His mutant could act as a translation repressor (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: The claim is based on in vitro translation assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gly172His in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A restores the gain-of-function mechanism of RocA.
source: These data indicated that Gly172His in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A restores the gain-of-function mechanism of RocA.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro translation assay data.

claim: No significant growth defects resulted from genetic manipulations of C. orbiculare eIF4A.
source: Notably, we did not find any significant growth defects resulting from these genetic manipulations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is based on colony growth assay data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Aglafoline resulted in essentially the same molecular phenotype of ATP-independent polypurine clamping of the Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A as RocA.
source: As expected, aglafoline resulted in essentially the same molecular phenotype of ATP-independent polypurine clamping of the Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H and Table 1) as RocA (Figure 2C, right, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–H; and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence polarization assay data comparing aglafoline and RocA.

claim: A subset of mRNAs showed high aglafoline sensitivity in terms of translation efficiency in conidia.
source: Consistent with the mRNA-selective action of the compound, we observed that a subset of mRNAs showed high aglafoline sensitivity in terms of translation efficiency in conidia (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The reduction in translation efficiency was compound dose dependent.
source: and that the reduction was compound dose dependent (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Genes associated with the ribosome and its assembly were susceptible to rocaglate-mediated translational repression.
source: Intriguingly, we observed that genes associated with the ribosome and its assembly were susceptible to rocaglate-mediated translational repression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on GO term analysis of ribosome profiling data.

claim: The reduction in translation efficiency mediated by aglafoline was attenuated by the His153Gly substitution.
source: The reduction in translation efficiency mediated by aglafoline was attenuated by the His153Gly substitution (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The reduction in translation efficiency was associated with the presence of polypurine motifs in the 5′ UTR.
source: Consistent with earlier reports (Chen et al., 2021; Chu et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2019; Iwasaki et al., 2016; Iwasaki et al., 2019), the reduction in translation efficiency was associated with the presence of polypurine motifs in the 5′ UTR (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3G and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The His153Gly substitution compromised the polypurine-dependent translational repression.
source: However, the His153Gly substitution compromised the polypurine-dependent translational repression.
evidence: The claim is based on ribosome profiling data.

claim: The mycelial stage of the fungus showed similar trends in translational repression mediated by aglafoline.
source: Although the mycelial stage of the fungus showed the similar trends in translational repression mediated by aglafoline (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–F)
evidence: The claim is based on ribosome profiling data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The sensitive mRNAs in mycelia were distinct from those in conidia.
source: the sensitive mRNAs were distinct from those in conidia (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G), suggesting differential impacts of rocaglates during the fungal life cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on ribosome profiling data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Aglafoline reduced the biomass of the WT eIF4A-recombined strain on cucumber leaves.
source: Indeed, aglafoline reduced the biomass of the WT eIF4A-recombined strain on cucumber leaves, showing the antifungal effect of rocaglate (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on RT-qPCR data measuring fungal biomass shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The His153Gly mutation in eIF4A affected fungal growth on cucumber leaves and resulted in rocaglate resistance in the fungi.
source: In stark contrast, the His153Gly mutation in eIF4A affected fungal growth on cucumber leaves and resulted in rocaglate resistance in the fungi (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on RT-qPCR data measuring fungal biomass shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The differential biomass of C. orbiculare could not be explained by the damage to cucumber leaves by aglafoline treatment.
source: We note that the differential biomass of C. orbiculare could not be explained by the damage to cucumber leaves by aglafoline treatment as no morphological alteration of the leaves was observed under our conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of cucumber leaves shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The Gly substitution found in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A provides the molecular basis of antirocaglate properties.
source: These results demonstrated that the Gly substitution found in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A provides the molecular basis of antirocaglate properties and allows the growth of the parasitic fungus in the presence of rocaglate (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Rocaglates are small molecules synthesized in plants of the genus Aglaia.
source: Rocaglates, small molecules synthesized in plants of the genus Aglaia, exemplify antifungal secondary metabolites (Engelmeier et al., 2000; Iyer et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rocaglates have antifungal properties.
source: Rocaglates, small molecules synthesized in plants of the genus Aglaia, exemplify antifungal secondary metabolites (Engelmeier et al., 2000; Iyer et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rocaglates have antitumor activities.
source: In addition to its antifungal properties, this group of compounds is of particular interest because of its antitumor activities (Alachkar et al., 2013; Bordeleau et al., 2008; Cencic et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2019; Ernst et al., 2020; Lucas et al., 2009; Manier et al., 2017; Nishida et al., 2021; Santagata et al., 2013; Skofler et al., 2021; Thompson et al., 2021; Thompson et al., 2017; Wilmore et al., 2021; Wolfe et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Recent studies have suggested rocaglates have potency against viruses such as SARS-CoV-2.
source: Moreover, recent studies have suggested potency against viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 (Müller et al., 2021; Müller et al., 2020) and hepatitis E virus (Praditya et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Recent studies have suggested rocaglates have potency against hepatitis E virus.
source: Moreover, recent studies have suggested potency against viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 (Müller et al., 2021; Müller et al., 2020) and hepatitis E virus (Praditya et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Rocaglates target translation initiation factor (eIF) 4A.
source: Rocaglates target translation initiation factor (eIF) 4A, a DEAD-box RNA binding protein, and function as potent translation inhibitors with a unique mechanism
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: eIF4A is a DEAD-box RNA binding protein.
source: Rocaglates target translation initiation factor (eIF) 4A, a DEAD-box RNA binding protein, and function as potent translation inhibitors with a unique mechanism
evidence: The claim is established knowledge about eIF4A.

claim: Rocaglate treatment does not phenocopy the loss of function of eIF4A but instead leads to gain of function.
source: rocaglate treatment does not phenocopy the loss of function of eIF4A but instead leads to gain of function.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rocaglates impose polypurine (A and G repeated) sequence selectivity on eIF4A.
source: Although eIF4A activates the translation of cellular mRNA through ATP-dependent RNA binding, rocaglates impose polypurine (A and G repeated) sequence selectivity on eIF4A, bypassing the ATP requirements and evoking mRNA-selective translational repression (Chen et al., 2021; Chu et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2019; Iwasaki et al., 2019; Iwasaki et al., 2016; Rubio et al., 2014; Wolfe et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Rocaglates bypass the ATP requirements of eIF4A.
source: Although eIF4A activates the translation of cellular mRNA through ATP-dependent RNA binding, rocaglates impose polypurine (A and G repeated) sequence selectivity on eIF4A, bypassing the ATP requirements and evoking mRNA-selective translational repression (Chen et al., 2021; Chu et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2019; Iwasaki et al., 2019; Iwasaki et al., 2016; Rubio et al., 2014; Wolfe et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Rocaglates evoke mRNA-selective translational repression.
source: Although eIF4A activates the translation of cellular mRNA through ATP-dependent RNA binding, rocaglates impose polypurine (A and G repeated) sequence selectivity on eIF4A, bypassing the ATP requirements and evoking mRNA-selective translational repression (Chen et al., 2021; Chu et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2019; Iwasaki et al., 2019; Iwasaki et al., 2016; Rubio et al., 2014; Wolfe et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The artificial anchoring of eIF4A becomes a steric hindrance to scanning 40S ribosomes.
source: The artificial anchoring of eIF4A (1) becomes a steric hindrance to scanning 40S ribosomes (Iwasaki et al., 2019; Iwasaki et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The artificial anchoring of eIF4A masks cap structure of mRNA by tethering eIF4F.
source: (2) masks cap structure of mRNA by tethering eIF4F (Chu et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The artificial anchoring of eIF4A reduces the available pool of eIF4A for active translation initiation events by the sequestration of eIF4A on mRNAs.
source: and (3) reduces the available pool of eIF4A for active translation initiation events by the sequestration of eIF4A on mRNAs (Chu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: eIF4A is an essential gene for all eukaryotes.
source: Since eIF4A is an essential gene for all eukaryotes, Aglaia plants must have a mechanism to evade the cytotoxicity of the rocaglates they produce.
evidence: The claim is established knowledge about eIF4A.

claim: Fungi that infect plants cause severe crop losses (~10%) worldwide.
source: Fungi that infect plants are of great economic relevance because they cause severe crop losses (~10%) worldwide (Oerke, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Secondary metabolites with antimicrobial activities are among the means naturally developed by plants for the control of fungal infections.
source: Secondary metabolites with antimicrobial activities are among the means naturally developed by plants for the control of fungal infections (Collemare et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Tomatine is a glycoalkaloid secreted from the leaves and stems of tomato.
source: For example, tomatine, a glycoalkaloid secreted from the leaves and stems of tomato, has both fungicidal properties and insecticidal activities (Vance et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Tomatine has both fungicidal properties and insecticidal activities.
source: For example, tomatine, a glycoalkaloid secreted from the leaves and stems of tomato, has both fungicidal properties and insecticidal activities (Vance et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Camalexin is an indole alkaloid produced by Brassicaceae plants.
source: Camalexin, an indole alkaloid produced by Brassicaceae plants, including the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, also has antifungal properties (Nafisi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Camalexin has antifungal properties.
source: Camalexin, an indole alkaloid produced by Brassicaceae plants, including the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, also has antifungal properties (Nafisi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The best-known strategy for fungi to overcome toxic compounds is the detoxification of antifungal compounds by the secretion of specific enzymes.
source: The best-known strategy is the detoxification of antifungal compounds by the secretion of specific enzymes (Crombie et al., 1986; Osbourn et al., 1995; Pareja-Jaime et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Plants and infectious fungi are engaged in an arms race during the course of evolution.
source: Thus, plants and infectious fungi are engaged in an arms race during the course of evolution.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the described interactions between plants and fungi.

claim: Other than detoxification, the mechanistic diversity of the plant–fungus competition centered on plant secondary metabolites is largely unknown.
source: However, other than detoxification, the mechanistic diversity of the plant–fungus competition centered on plant secondary metabolites is largely unknown.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Ophiocordyceps spp. are members of the phylum Ascomycota.
source: Ophiocordyceps spp. are members of the phylum Ascomycota and constitute the taxonomic groups with the highest number of entomopathogenic species among all fungal genera.
evidence: The claim is established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Ophiocordyceps constitute the taxonomic groups with the highest number of entomopathogenic species among all fungal genera.
source: Ophiocordyceps spp. are members of the phylum Ascomycota and constitute the taxonomic groups with the highest number of entomopathogenic species among all fungal genera.
evidence: The claim is established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Each Ophiocordyceps spp. has a specific host insect species in most cases.
source: In most cases, each Ophiocordyceps spp. has a specific host insect species, develops fruiting bodies from the remains of host insects, and produces spores.
evidence: The claim is established knowledge about Ophiocordyceps.

claim: Ophiocordyceps sinensis has been found to reside on many plant species.
source: In addition to insect infection, a moth parasite, Ophiocordyceps sinensis, has been found to reside on many plant species, suggesting that Ophiocordyceps also has an endophytic lifestyle (Wang et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ophiocordyceps also has an endophytic lifestyle.
source: In addition to insect infection, a moth parasite, Ophiocordyceps sinensis, has been found to reside on many plant species, suggesting that Ophiocordyceps also has an endophytic lifestyle (Wang et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The molecular basis of secondary metabolite resistance in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 is markedly distinct from the known strategies developed in other fungi.
source: The molecular basis of secondary metabolite resistance in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 is markedly distinct from the known strategies developed in other fungi.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the comparison with other fungal resistance mechanisms.

claim: Avenacin from oats is a triterpenoid that forms complexes with sterols in fungal cell membranes.
source: Avenacin from oats — an example of a plant-secreted antimicrobial substance (Morrissey and Osbourn, 1999) — is a triterpenoid that forms complexes with sterols in fungal cell membranes, causes a loss of membrane integrity, and thus exerts an antifungal effect (Armah et al., 1999; Osbourn et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Avenacin causes a loss of membrane integrity in fungi.
source: Avenacin from oats — an example of a plant-secreted antimicrobial substance (Morrissey and Osbourn, 1999) — is a triterpenoid that forms complexes with sterols in fungal cell membranes, causes a loss of membrane integrity, and thus exerts an antifungal effect (Armah et al., 1999; Osbourn et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gaeumannomyces graminis var. avenae secretes avenaciase to counteract avenacin and infect oats.
source: To counteract this compound and infect oats, the phytopathogenic fungus Gaeumannomyces graminis var. avenae (Gga) secretes avenaciase (Crombie et al., 1986; Osbourn et al., 1995), a β-glycosyl hydrolase that hydrolyzes terminal D-glucose in the sugar chain of avenacin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Avenaciase is a β-glycosyl hydrolase that hydrolyzes terminal D-glucose in the sugar chain of avenacin.
source: To counteract this compound and infect oats, the phytopathogenic fungus Gaeumannomyces graminis var. avenae (Gga) secretes avenaciase (Crombie et al., 1986; Osbourn et al., 1995), a β-glycosyl hydrolase that hydrolyzes terminal D-glucose in the sugar chain of avenacin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Avenacin degradation by avenaciase determines the host range of Gaeumannomyces graminis var. avenae.
source: Indeed, avenacin degradation by this enzyme determines the host range of the fungus (Bowyer et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 may cope with rocaglates through desensitization of the target protein eIF4A by an amino acid substitution.
source: In contrast to the detoxification strategy, Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 may cope with rocaglates through desensitization of the target protein eIF4A by an amino acid substitution (Figure 2), leaving the compound intact.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The different resistance mechanisms to toxic small molecules should be highly related to the compound targets.
source: The different resistance mechanisms to toxic small molecules should be highly related to the compound targets.
evidence: The claim is a general inference about resistance mechanisms.

claim: The conversion of target sterols to evade avenacin requires many enzyme modifications and occurs only rarely.
source: Since sterols targeted by avenacin are biosynthesized via complicated multiple steps with diverse enzymes, thus generating diverse sterol structures, the conversion of target sterols to evade avenacin requires many enzyme modifications and occurs only rarely.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the complexity of sterol biosynthesis.

claim: Evasion of rocaglates by a single amino acid mutation in eIF4A is relatively likely.
source: On the other hand, the target of rocaglates is an eIF4A protein (and a DDX3 protein, see below for details), and thus, evasion by a single amino acid mutation is relatively likely.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the nature of the target.

claim: The resistance of Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 to rocaglate may not be as complete as that obtained by the substitution found in Aglaia Phe163Leu.
source: Although we observed that Gly163 in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 eIF4A produced a substantial change in sensitivity to rocaglate, the resistance may not be as complete as that obtained by the substitution found in Aglaia Phe163Leu (Iwasaki et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison of Kd values and prior work.

claim: DDX3 was recently found to be an alternative target of rocaglate.
source: Additionally, the translation factor DDX3, which was recently found to be an alternative target of rocaglate (Chen et al., 2021), did not have amino acid substitutions in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: DDX3 did not have amino acid substitutions in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1.
source: Additionally, the translation factor DDX3, which was recently found to be an alternative target of rocaglate (Chen et al., 2021), did not have amino acid substitutions in Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Aglaia DDX3s harbor a substitution at Gln360.
source: whereas Aglaia DDX3s harbor a substitution at Gln360 (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 may still be in the process of evolving fitness for growth in Aglaia plants.
source: This may indicate that Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1 is still in the process of evolving fitness for growth in Aglaia plants.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the incomplete resistance.

source: This study showed that the parasitic fungus Ophiocordyceps sp. BRM1, which possibly originates from Ophiocordyceps spp. with an endophytic life stage, on Aglaia could also overcome this barrier by introducing an amino acid conversion (Phe163Gly) in eIF4A (Figure 5, bottom).

claim: Ribosome profiling is a technique based on deep sequencing of ribosome-protected RNA fragments generated by RNase treatment.
source: To understand the translational repression induced by aglafoline in a genome-wide manner, we applied ribosome profiling, a technique based on deep sequencing of ribosome-protected RNA fragments (i.e., ribosome footprints) generated by RNase treatment (Ingolia et al., 2019; Ingolia et al., 2009; Iwasaki and Ingolia, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work describing the technique.

evidence: The claim is based on ribosome profiling data shown in supplementary figures.
